You do not need to turn this service on: the shortcut turns it on when needed and it turns itself off when you leave the rescue.\n\nWhy it needs full control: to read the screen with its own voice when your screen reader is silent, to get the volume keys during the rescue, to raise the accessibility volume and to guide you through Settings. It never stores or sends anything it reads.

Optional. Stays on and checks, without reading the screen, whether your screen reader and the system voice still work. If your screen reader turns off or the system voice stops speaking, it warns you with the rescue voice, reads the screen with it (echo mode) and lets you open the rescue by pressing volume up three times quickly. It never stores or sends anything.

1. In Settings, Accessibility, open Accessible Rescue (it may be under Downloaded apps or Installed services).
2. Turn on «Accessible Rescue shortcut» and choose «Hold volume keys». Do not turn the service itself on: the shortcut does it when needed.
3. Make Accessible Rescue the only feature on that shortcut: with more, Android asks which one to use, and without a screen reader that question is not spoken.
4. In the shortcut settings, leave it allowed from the lock screen.

If Android says the setting is restricted (Android 13 or later, when the APK was installed from a browser or a file manager): open the Accessible Rescue app info, More options menu, «Allow restricted settings», and come back here.

2. Turn it on and, in «Shortcut service», choose Accessible Rescue.
3. Leave «Allow from lock screen» on.
4. Do not turn on the Accessible Rescue service by hand: the shortcut does it when needed.

The guardian is a second Accessible Rescue service that stays on. It does not read the screen: it checks whether your screen reader or the system voice stop working and, if so, warns you with the rescue voice, reads the screen with it and lets you open the rescue by pressing volume up three times quickly.\n\nIn Settings, Accessibility, open «Accessible Rescue: guardian» and turn it on. Android will ask to allow full control: it needs it to read in echo mode and to get the volume keys. You turn it off in the same place.

Accessible Rescue helps you get your screen reader, voice and accessibility back with no one's help. It has its own voice, with no Internet, that speaks even if the system one fails.

Now, with your screen reader working, you will set it up in a few steps. Each one explains what it does and why. You can repeat this assistant whenever you want.

Choose the app language (it can differ from the phone's):
The app has its own voice (Pico and, also, eSpeak NG). It does not use the system speech engine or the Internet, so it speaks even if those fail. Test it. If you do not hear it, turn the volume up.
Use Pico as the rescue voice (recommended)
Use eSpeak NG as the rescue voice

The first time you use the shortcut, Android asks whether to use it and warns that Accessible Rescue will be able to view and control the screen («full control»).

Why it needs it: to read the screen with its voice when your screen reader is silent, to get the volume keys during the rescue, to raise the accessibility volume and to guide you through Settings.

What it does not do: it does not store, log or send anything it reads; it does not run in the background except the guardian, if you turn it on; it changes nothing you did not ask for.

How to remove it: in Settings, Accessibility, by removing the shortcut or turning the service off, or by uninstalling the app.

Hold both volume keys together for about three seconds. The first time, Android asks whether to use the shortcut: your screen reader reads it to you; accept it. The rescue menu opens: listen to the introduction, explore it and leave with Leave the rescue. You can also open it with the button below.

Android only lets an app turn screen readers on or off and change the speech engine with a permission granted once (WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGS). With it, the rescue makes those changes at once and has full safe mode, like Shortcut Menu. Without it, the rescue guides you through Settings. It can be granted from the phone itself with wireless debugging, with a computer or with root.

So that the guardian can alert you with a notification and Android does not close the app to save battery. Both are optional: the guardian also warns with the voice. Some phones (Xiaomi, Huawei, OPPO, vivo) also have an «Autostart» setting worth allowing for this app and for TalkBack.
Do not optimize this app\'s battery

Saves on the phone a copy of TalkBack and the Google voice as they are now, working. If one day they break or an update fails, the rescue reinstalls them without the Internet or a store. They take a few hundred megabytes.

Silently checks that your current speech engine really speaks and remembers it as «the one that works». If one day someone changes the engine or it breaks, the rescue can go back to it. Remember that the rescue can also set its own voice as the system voice.
Saves how your accessibility is now (screen reader, speech engine, rate, shortcuts) to go back to it with «Restore my settings». It also records the rescue backup messages.
This is how your rescue stands. If something is missing, tap it to fix it. When you need it: hold both volume keys. If your screen reader is silent, press volume up three times quickly in the menu.

Hello. The person who uses this phone is blind, and their screen reader or voice has stopped working. This screen explains how to help. Brightness is at maximum.
What is wrong with the phone
1. Open accessibility settings (button below) and check that %1$s is on. If not, turn it on and accept the warning.
2. If it is on but silent, open the speech settings (button below) and choose «Rescue voice (Pico)» or another working engine as the preferred engine. Check the volume is high.
3. If Bluetooth headphones are connected, disconnect them.
4. With the screen reader on, the screen works differently: tap once to select and twice quickly to press; swipe with two fingers to scroll.
Accessible Rescue %1$s. Made by XeBoLaX with the work of other people, whom it thanks.

The idea of the self-speaking shortcut menu, the safe mode with three presses of volume up that turns screen readers off and gives them back, switching screen readers and speech engines with the advanced permission, and the use of Pico come from Shortcut Menu, by aaron-gh (github.com/aaron-gh/shortcut-menu), under the Apache 2.0 license. Accessible Rescue includes modified code from it; each derived file says so. All rights to that solution belong to its author.
Speech engine by SVOX AG, from the Android Open Source Project, under the Apache 2.0 license. Spanish, US English and British English voices.
eSpeak NG 1.52.0 speech engine, by Reece H. Dunn and contributors, under the GPL 3 or later. Includes ucd-tools and speech-player.
